entry.title: Two-dimensional stealthy hyperuniform polycrystalline disk packings
entry.summary:
Author(s): Carlo Vanoni, Paul J. Steinhardt, and Salvatore Torquato Polycrystals normally break hyperuniformity: randomly sized and oriented grains create long-wavelength density fluctuations. Here, the authors use collective-coordinate optimization to build two-dimensional disk packings that are polycrystalline yet ultradense, stealthy, and hyperuniform. Compared with dense, nonhyperuniform polycrystalline packings produced by standard compression algorithms, their packings show a distinctive grain-size distribution reflecting long-range grain correlations, perfect transparency to electromagnetic waves at small wave vectors, and enhanced diffusion spreadability. Although unlikely to form naturally, they could be realized through nanolithography or 3D printing as optical and transport metamaterials.

entry.title: Interparticle collision dynamics and its impact on turbulence in horizontal channel flow
entry.summary:
Author(s): Jinchi Li, Yicong Zhu, Xiaojing Zheng, and Ping Wang Inter-particle collisions are often neglected in dilute particle-laden wall turbulence, yet turbulent clustering can raise local concentrations far above the mean. Using four-way coupled point-particle DNS of a horizontal open channel, we show that collisions modulate turbulence in qualitatively opposite ways depending on gravity. Without gravity, collisions of inertial particles occur near vortex edges, generating extra velocity fluctuations and enhancing turbulence. With gravity, collisions of heavy particles concentrate near vortex cores, suppressing wall rebound, ejection and hairpin vortices, and further attenuating turbulence — an effect that strengthens with particle inertia.

entry.title: Semiclassical study of muon-enhanced proton-$^{11}\mathrm{B}$ fusion
entry.summary:
Author(s): Hong-Yi Wang (王弘毅), Ming-Yu Chen (陈铭宇), Hao-Le Ma (马好乐), and Zhu-Fang Cui (崔著钫) Proton–boron-11 (p–11B) fusion only converts its reactants into three charged α particles, so that is an attractive aneutronic path to fusion energy, but the high Coulomb barrier of the 11B nucleus (Z = 5) keeps its reactivity low. We study a new pathway that form a muonic hydrogen atom (pμ) first, whose Bohr radius is about 200 times smaller than ordinary hydrogen, then bombard it with a 11B nucleus. We simulate the full three-body classical motion with the classical trajectory Monte Carlo method, sampling the pμ initial state from the microcanonical ground-state ensemble. From the statistical distribution of classical turning points, we compute the Coulomb-barrier tunneling probability and obtain the cross section. The results show that the μ enhances the low-energy cross section by several orders of magnitude compared with bare nuclei. Thus, if combined with intense laser fields or high-density compression, this mechanism may enable low-energy auxiliary ignition of aneutronic p–11B fusion.
[Phys. Rev. C 114, 054609] Published Thu Nov 19, 2026

Author(s): Quoc Hoan Tran, Koki Chinzei, Yasuhiro Endo, and Hirotaka Oshima At the intersection of machine learning and quantum information, quantum diffusion models learn a distribution of quantum states by gradually scrambling it and then learning to reverse the process, offering a fresh route to generating quantum data for chemical and materials research. The authors demonstrate this with a model trained on cubic CsPbI3 slab configurations that reproduces the temperature-driven orthorhombic-tetragonal-cubic phase transitions in bulk CsPbI3. entry.title: Evolution of the saddle point in antimony telluride homologous superlattices
entry.summary:
Author(s): Yi-Hsin Shen, Shane Smolenski, Ming Wen, Yimo Hou, Nishkarsh Agarwal, Eoghan Downey, Jakob Hammond-Renfro, Katharine Moncrieffe, Chun Lin, Makoto Hashimoto, Donghui Lu, Robert Hovden, Kai Sun, Dominika Zgid, Emanuel Gull, Pierre Ferdinand P. Poudeu, Na Hyun Jo, and Rachel S. Goldman Engineering the density of states near the Fermi level is a central strategy for accessing correlated quantum matter, with broad implications for emerging electronic and quantum technologies. One particularly powerful route involves saddle points in the electronic band structure, which give rise to van Hove singularities (VHSs) with divergent density of states. To date, approaches for bringing the Fermi level into alignment with a VHS have relied mainly upon gating, chemical doping, or heterostructure engineering. Here, the authors demonstrate an alternative pathway - combining topological insulators (antimony telluride) with topological semimetals (antimonene) in the form of antimony telluride homologous superlattices. Using scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS) and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), in conjunction with scGW calculations, they provide evidence for a saddle point and associated van Hove singularity near the M-point. They identify the key role of Sb and Te pz orbital hybridization in generating the saddle point and shifting it toward the Fermi level as the number of antimonene layers increases. These findings establish a pathway for tuning van Hove singularities through atomic-layer engineering, offering new opportunities for realizing correlated quantum phases.
[Phys. Rev. Materials 10, 114003] Published Mon Nov 16, 2026

So far, these effects have been understood to be governed primarily by the interfacial magnetization. In this work, the authors go beyond this picture by demonstrating that magnetic order deeper within a multilayer CrI₃ magnet can also influence an adjacent WSe₂ semiconductor. While the neutral exciton valley splitting in WSe₂ tracks the interfacial CrI₃ magnetization, the optical response of positively charged trions is additionally sensitive to the magnetic alignment of more distant CrI₃ layers. These findings open new perspectives for engineering spin and valley properties in van der Waals heterostructures.

entry.title: Conductivity of a non-Galilean-invariant Fermi liquid: Exact solution of the kinetic equation
entry.summary:
Author(s): Tatia Kiliptari, Vladimir I. Yudson, and Dmitrii L. Maslov In a Fermi liquid, the quasiparticle scattering rate scales as T2, whereas the low-temperature correction to the residual resistivity can scale as T4, seemingly implying a strongly suppressed current-relaxation rate. The authors resolve this paradox here by solving the kinetic equation exactly for a disordered, non-Galilean-invariant Fermi liquid. They show that electron–electron collisions enter the conductivity through the quasiparticle scattering time itself, which controls the crossover between collisionless and hydrodynamic transport. The extra T2 factor arises because momentum conservation makes the change in the total velocity of two colliding electrons vanish on the Fermi surface, so current relaxation comes only from thermally excited states away from it. The electron–electron contribution to the dc conductivity nevertheless remains parametrically small throughout the Fermi-liquid regime. By extrapolating the result toward a z=3 quantum critical point, the authors further show that the renormalized quasiparticle scattering rate saturates the Planckian bound.
[Phys. Rev. B 114, L291103] Published Thu Nov 12, 2026

Lange, G. Peng, S. Rothe, A. Schmidt, C. Schweiger, and J. Wessolek The delivery of radioactive ion beams of refractory elements using the ISOL method remains challenging, limiting access to isotopes for nuclear-structure studies. We demonstrate a method to overcome this limitation using in-trap β− decay in the ISCOOL radiofrequency quadrupole trap at CERN-ISOLDE. Radioactive parent ions are confined in helium buffer gas, where their decay products can be slowed, captured and extracted as an ion beam. Using 97,98Rb and 98Sr, we produce 97,98Sr and 98Y, monitoring their populations as a function of trapping time with the ISOLTRAP multi-reflection time-of-flight mass spectrometer. Fits to Bateman decay equations reproduce the known half-lives, validating the method and demonstrating daughter-beam efficiencies of approximately 1% relative to the initial parent intensity. We report the first delivery of a singly charged atomic 98Y beam at ISOLDE. This approach requires no modification to the existing target or ion source and opens new opportunities to study refractory isotopes that are otherwise difficult to extract.
